claim: 60–90% of a cell's cholesterol is concentrated in its plasma membrane (PM)
source: Although present in the membrane of every organelle, 60–90% of a cell's cholesterol is concentrated in its plasma membrane (PM) (De Duve, 1971; Lange et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Duve, 1971 and Lange et al., 1989

claim: In the PM, the concentration of cholesterol is ~45 mole% of total lipids
source: In the PM, the concentration of cholesterol is ~45 mole% of total lipids (Das et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Das et al., 2013

claim: Cells acquire cholesterol through receptor-mediated endocytosis of cholesterol-rich low-density lipoprotein (LDL)
source: Much has been learned about the two sources through which cells acquire cholesterol – (i) receptor-mediated endocytosis of cholesterol-rich low-density lipoprotein (LDL) (Brown and Goldstein, 1986)
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown and Goldstein, 1986

claim: Cells acquire cholesterol through biosynthesis
source: Much has been learned about the two sources through which cells acquire cholesterol – (i) receptor-mediated endocytosis of cholesterol-rich low-density lipoprotein (LDL) (Brown and Goldstein, 1986), and (ii) biosynthesis (Brown and Goldstein, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown and Goldstein, 1990

claim: The SREBP regulatory network that controls rates of LDL uptake and cholesterol biosynthesis is located in the ER
source: Moreover, the SREBP regulatory network that controls rates of LDL uptake and cholesterol biosynthesis is located not in the PM, but in the ER (Brown and Goldstein, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown and Goldstein, 2009

claim: One pool of PM cholesterol, ~15 mole% of PM lipids, is sequestered by sphingomyelin
source: These studies showed that one pool of PM cholesterol, ~15 mole% of PM lipids, is sequestered by sphingomyelin.
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous studies referenced in the context (Das et al., 2014)

claim: A second pool of PM cholesterol, ~12 mole% of PM lipids, is sequestered by other membrane factors
source: A second pool, ~12 mole% of PM lipids, is sequestered by other membrane factors.
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous studies referenced in the context (Das et al., 2014)

claim: Cholesterol in excess of the two sequestered pools comprises a third pool that signals cholesterol excess to the regulatory machinery in the ER
source: Cholesterol in excess of these two sequestered pools comprises a third pool that signals cholesterol excess to the regulatory machinery in the ER, thereby avoiding cholesterol overaccumulation while ensuring optimal cholesterol levels in PM.
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous studies referenced in the context (Das et al., 2014)

claim: Recombinant ALOD4 elutes as a single sharp peak in gel-filtration chromatography
source: Gel-filtration chromatography of purified ALOD4 showed that it eluted as a single sharp peak (Figure 1A, blue), and its homogeneity was confirmed by Coomassie staining (Figure 1A inset).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: ALOD4 does not lyse CHO-K1 cells at 37°C
source: When added to CHO-K1 cells, ALOFL permeabilized the PM as revealed by immunoblotting of the medium for two cytosolic proteins, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and ubiquitin-activating enzyme (E1) (Figure 1B, lanes 2–4). Similar release of cytosolic content was observed when the cells were lysed with SDS (Figure 1B, lane 9); however, no such effect was observed when cells were treated with ALOD4, even at the highest concentration of 10 µM (Figure 1B, lanes 6–8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B comparing ALOFL and ALOD4 effects

claim: Binding of ALOD4 to PMs triggers activation of SREBPs in CHO-K1 cells
source: As increasing amounts of ALOD4 bound to these cells, we detected increasing amounts of the proteolyzed nuclear forms of both SREBP2 and SREBP1, and a corresponding decline in their precursor forms (Figure 2A, second and third panels, lanes 1–7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: ALOD4 triggers activation of SREBP1 and SREBP2 in human fibroblast cells (SV-589)
source: ALOD4 also triggered the activation of SREBP1 and SREBP2 in human fibroblast cells (SV-589) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: ALOD4's triggering of SREBP2 activation requires its binding to PM cholesterol
source: As shown in Figure 3A, when incubated with CHO-K1 cells, ALOD4 bound to cells (top panel, lanes 1–4) and triggered activation of SREBP2 (middle panel, lanes 1–4), whereas ALOD4(Mut) did not bind to cells (top panel, lanes 5–8) or trigger activation of SREBP2 (middle panel, lanes 5–8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing ALOD4 and ALOD4(Mut) in Figure 3A

claim: HPCD treatment lowers total cellular cholesterol from ~30 µg/mg protein to ~18 µg/mg protein
source: The HPCD-induced increase in SREBP2 processing was accompanied by a decrease in total cellular cholesterol from ~30 µg/mg protein to ~18 µg/mg protein (Figure 3C, lanes 1–3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: ALOD4-induced increase in SREBP2 processing occurs without significant change in total cellular cholesterol
source: However, the ALOD4-induced increase in SREBP2 processing was observed even though there was no significant change in total cellular cholesterol (Figure 3C, lanes 4–6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: ALOD4 triggers SREBP2 activation by binding to PM cholesterol and preventing its transport to ER
source: Together, the experiments of Figure 3 suggest that ALOD4 triggers SREBP2 activation by binding to PM cholesterol and preventing its transport to ER, and not by blocking lipoprotein uptake or depleting cellular cholesterol.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations in Figure 3

claim: ALOD4 treatment increases mRNA levels of HMG CoA Reductase and LDL receptor genes
source: As shown in Figure 3D, expression of mRNAs for both these SREBP target genes was increased by ALOD4 treatment, and these increases were similar to that observed after HPCD treatment.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Fluorescently-labeled versions of ALOD4 (fALOD4-488 and fALOD4-647) trigger SREBP2 activation with the same concentration dependence as ALOD4
source: fluorescently-labeled versions of ALOD4 that trigger SREBP2 activation in CHO-K1 cells with the same concentration dependence as ALOD4 (Figure 4A, compare lanes 1–4 to lanes 5–8 and lanes 9–12).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: ALOD4 binds rapidly to CHO-K1 cells with half-maximal binding at 10 min and saturation at 40 min
source: We detected rapid binding of ALOD4, both by immunoblot analysis (Figure 4B, upper panel, lanes 1–7) and by fluorescence measurements (Figure 4C, black filled circles). Half-maximal binding occurred at 10 min and saturation was reached after 40 min.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 4C

claim: There is a lag time of approximately 60 min before ALOD4 binding triggers SREBP2 activation
source: Once ALOD4 bound to PMs, there was a lag time before triggering of SREBP2 activation at 60 min (Figure 4B, lower panel, lanes 1–7, and densitometry quantification in Figure 4C, red filled circles).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 4C

claim: ALOD4(Mut) shows no significant binding to PMs
source: As a control, ALOD4(Mut) showed no significant binding to PMs (Figure 4B, upper panel, lanes 8–14, and Figure 4C, black open circles)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 4C

claim: ALOD4 dissociates rapidly from PMs with ~90% detaching within 5 min
source: Dissociation of this bound ALOD4 was rapid, with ~90% detaching from cells within 5 min (Figure 4D, lower panel, lanes 2–6 and 8–12, and Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D and 4E

claim: ALOD4 treatment lowers ER cholesterol from ~8 mole% to ~4 mole% of total ER lipids
source: The ER cholesterol content of FCS-treated cells was ~8 mole% of total ER lipids and this value declined by a similar degree to ~4 mole% of total ER lipids when treated with ALOD4 or HPCD (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: ALOD4 treatment does not significantly alter cholesterol levels in the whole cell or in PM
source: Compared to the FCS-treated set, ALOD4 treatment did not significantly alter cholesterol levels in the whole cell or in PM, whereas HPCD treatment lowered total cellular cholesterol from ~33 µg/mg protein to ~20 µg/mg protein and PM cholesterol from 41 mole% of total PM lipids to ~31 mole% of total PM lipids (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: HPCD treatment lowers PM cholesterol from 41 mole% to ~31 mole% of total PM lipids
source: HPCD treatment lowered total cellular cholesterol from ~33 µg/mg protein to ~20 µg/mg protein and PM cholesterol from 41 mole% of total PM lipids to ~31 mole% of total PM lipids (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: LDL-derived cholesterol travels from lysosomes directly to PM
source: At the PM, ALOD4 sequestered the LDL-derived cholesterol, preventing it from traveling to the ER and suppressing SREBP2 activation (Figure 6A), or stimulating the activity of ACAT (Figure 6B). These data support the model that LDL-derived cholesterol moves first from lysosomes to PM (Figure 9).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6A and 6B, and inferred from the observation that ALOD4 at PM blocks LDL-derived cholesterol from reaching ER

claim: ALOD4 completely blocks LDL-mediated suppression of SREBP2 activation
source: Incubation with increasing amounts of LDL for 3 hr suppressed SREBP2 activation, leading to a decrease in the cleaved nuclear form and a corresponding increase in the uncleaved precursor form (Figure 6A, top panel lanes 2–4). However, addition of 3 µM ALOD4 during the 3 hr LDL incubation period completely blocked the suppression of SREBP2 activation, and only the cleaved nuclear form was detected (Figure 6A, top panel lanes 5–8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: As increasing amounts of LDL are added to sterol-depleted cells, PM-bound ALOD4 increases
source: After cholesterol depletion, no binding of ALOD4 was detected (Figure 6A, bottom panel, lane 5), indicating levels of accessible PM cholesterol were low. As increasing amounts of LDL were added, a steady increase in PM-bound ALOD4 was observed, indicating a rise in levels of accessible PM cholesterol (Figure 6A, bottom panel lanes 6–8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: ALOD4 completely blocks LDL-derived cholesterol from stimulating ACAT activity
source: As shown in Figure 6B, cholesteryl [14C]oleate formation increased in a dose-dependent manner as increasing amounts of LDL were added (left panel, black filled circles), but was completely blocked when 3 µM ALOD4 was included during the incubation with LDL and [14C]oleate (left panel, red filled circles).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: ALOD4 has little effect on 25-HC mediated cholesteryl [14C]oleate formation
source: In contrast to the all-or-none effects observed with LDL, ALOD4 had little effect on 25-HC mediated cholesteryl [14C]oleate formation (Figure 6B, right panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Cholesterol-binding toxins like ALOD4 do not bind 25-HC
source: This is likely because cholesterol-binding toxins like ALOD4 do not bind 25-HC (Sokolov and Radhakrishnan, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sokolov and Radhakrishnan, 2010

claim: ALOD4 does not inhibit the uptake or degradation of LDL
source: As shown in Figure 6C, when incubated at 37°C, the uptake of [125I]LDL increased as increasing concentrations of ALOD4 were added (left panel), a result that is consistent with increased expression of the LDL receptor induced by ALOD4 treatment (Figure 3D). The degradation of [125I]LDL persisted even at the highest added concentration of 3 µM ALOD4 (Figure 6C, right panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: In NPC1-deficient cells, LDL-derived cholesterol does not reach the PM to fill up its pool of accessible cholesterol
source: In NPC1-deficient cells, LDL-derived cholesterol does not reach the PM to fill up its pool of accessible cholesterol (Das et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Das et al., 2013

claim: LDL is unable to stimulate cholesterol esterification in NPC1-deficient cells
source: Consistent with previous studies, we also show here that LDL was unable to stimulate cholesterol esterification in these NPC1-deficient cells (Figure 7A, black bars).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: 25-HC stimulates cholesterol esterification in both control and NPC1-deficient cells
source: In contrast, stimulation of cholesterol esterification by 25-HC occurred in both control and NPC1-deficient cells (Figure 7A, gray bars).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: ALOD4 triggers SREBP2 activation in NPC1-deficient cells with identical concentration dependence as in control cells
source: We observed similar binding of ALOD4 to their PMs (Figure 7B, bottom panel, compare lanes 1–4 to lanes 5–8) and identical concentration dependences for triggering SREBP2 activation (Figure 7B, top panel, compare lanes 1–4 to lanes 5–8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: The pool of PM cholesterol that is transported to ER to suppress SREBP2 activation is of similar magnitude in control and NPC1-deficient cells
source: This result suggests that the pool of PM cholesterol that is transported to ER to suppress SREBP2 activation is of a similar magnitude in control and NPC1-deficient cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ALOD4 triggers SREBP2 activation with identical concentration dependence in both cell types

claim: HPCD treatment overcomes the inability of NPC1-deficient cells to transport LDL-derived cholesterol out of lysosomes to ER
source: LDL treatment also suppressed the activation of SREBP2 in NPC1-deficient cells (lower panel, lanes 1–4). This paradoxical result is consistent with an earlier study where HPCD treatment overcame the inability of NPC1-deficient cells to transport LDL-derived cholesterol out of lysosomes to ER (Abi-Mosleh et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abi-Mosleh et al., 2009 and experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: ALOD4 does not overcome the post-lysosomal cholesterol trafficking defect caused by NPC1-deficiency
source: Rapid dissociation of ALOD4 from PMs (Figure 4C–D) allowed LDL-derived cholesterol to transit through the PM and reach the ER to suppress the activation of SREBP2 in control cells (Figure 7C, upper panel, lanes 5–8), but not in NPC1-deficient cells (Figure 7C, lower panel, lanes 5–8). Thus, unlike HPCD, ALOD4 does not overcome the post-lysosomal cholesterol trafficking defect caused by NPC1-deficiency.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Cholesterol/MCD complexes deliver cholesterol directly to PM
source: After cholesterol depletion, no binding of ALOD4 was detected (Figure 8A, bottom panel lane 1), indicating levels of accessible PM cholesterol were low. As increasing amounts of cholesterol/MCD were added, we observed an increase in PM-bound ALOD4 (Figure 8A, bottom panel lanes 1–4), indicating that levels of accessible PM cholesterol had increased. This suggests that cholesterol/MCD complexes deliver their cholesterol to the PM
evidence: Inferred from the observation that cholesterol/MCD addition increases PM-bound ALOD4

claim: ALOD4 prevents cholesterol delivered by MCD complexes from moving to the ER to suppress SREBP activation
source: This activation of SREBP2 was suppressed when we added cholesterol/MCD complexes (Figure 8A, top panel, lanes 1–4), but suppression was blocked in the presence of 3 µM ALOD4 (Figure 8A, middle panel, lanes 1–4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A

claim: ALOD4 has no effect on the ability of 25-HC to suppress SREBP2 activation
source: In contrast, ALOD4 had no effect on the ability of 25-HC to suppress SREBP2 activation (Figure 8A, top and middle panels, lanes 5–8)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A

claim: 25-HC suppresses SREBP2 transport to Golgi by binding to Insigs, not to Scap
source: 25-HC suppresses SREBP2 transport to Golgi by binding not to the cholesterol sensor Scap, but to Insigs, ER retention proteins (Radhakrishnan et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Radhakrishnan et al., 2007

claim: ALOD4's ability to sequester cholesterol delivered to PM in MCD complexes can be saturated
source: Supplementation with 100 µM and 200 µM cholesterol/MCD delivered even more cholesterol to PM, as judged by further increases in bound ALOD4 (bottom panel, lanes 7 and 8). In these cases, the additional cholesterol in PM was in excess of ALOD4's sequestering capacity, leading to transport of cholesterol to ER and suppression of SREBP2 activation (top panel, lanes 7 and 8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B

claim: ALOD4 is not internalized by cells during the treatment conditions used in the study
source: We observed no bound ALOD4 in the condition where cholesterol was added (middle panel, lane 6), suggesting that all of the PM-bound ALOD4 had dissociated during the 40 min period and that no detectable level of ALOD4 had been internalized during the 3 hr incubation period.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C

claim: Sequestering approximately 1% of cellular cholesterol at the PM can trigger activation of SREBPs
source: While being mindful of the many assumptions made in estimating these values, our results suggest that sequestering just a small fraction (~1%) of cellular cholesterol at the PM and preventing its movement to ER, can trigger activation of SREBPs in an all-or-none manner.
evidence: Inferred from calculations based on ALOD4 binding measurements and cellular cholesterol content

claim: At saturation, ~150 ng (~10 pmol) of ALOD4 binds to ~120,000 CHO-K1 cells
source: At saturation, ~150 ng (~10 pmol) of ALOD4 bound to ~120,000 cells in a single well of a 48-well plate (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: A CHO-K1 cell contains approximately 10 fmol of cholesterol
source: In an earlier study, we estimated that a CHO-K1 cell growing in lipoprotein-rich FCS contains ~10 fmol of cholesterol (Radhakrishnan et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Radhakrishnan et al., 2008

claim: When ER cholesterol is above a threshold value of 5 mole% of ER lipids, cholesterol binds to Scap leading to formation of a complex with Insigs
source: In cells replete with cholesterol, robust PM-to-ER cholesterol transport ensures that the ER cholesterol concentration is above a threshold value of 5 mole% of ER lipids (Radhakrishnan et al., 2008). At these high concentrations, cholesterol binds to the ER cholesterol sensor Scap, leading to formation of a complex with ER-resident Insigs, thus preventing Scap's recruitment into CopII coated vesicles and transport of SREBPs to Golgi where they can be proteolytically activated (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Radhakrishnan et al., 2008 and established knowledge of SREBP regulation

claim: Incubating cholesterol-replete cells with ALOD4 for 1 hr results in ER cholesterol dropping below the threshold concentration of 5 mole%
source: Incubating these cholesterol-replete cells with ALOD4 for 1 hr in the presence of compactin, an inhibitor of cholesterol synthesis, results in ER cholesterol dropping below the threshold concentration of 5 mole% (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: When cells are replete with cholesterol, the ER continuously receives cholesterol from PM to offset losses of cholesterol due to efflux out of ER
source: This suggests that when cells are replete with cholesterol, the ER continuously receives cholesterol from PM to offset losses of cholesterol due to efflux out of ER.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking PM-to-ER transport with ALOD4 causes ER cholesterol to drop below threshold

claim: Continuous PM-to-ER cholesterol transport allows the ER to constantly sample the cholesterol content of PMs
source: This allows the ER to constantly sample the cholesterol content of PMs, and make adjustments via transcriptional regulation of cholesterol uptake and synthesis to ensure optimal PM cholesterol levels.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking PM-to-ER transport triggers SREBP activation

claim: Cells from individuals with familial hypercholesterolemia revealed how LDL receptors enable the uptake of cholesterol-rich LDL by receptor-mediated endocytosis
source: Cells from individuals with familial hypercholesterolemia revealed how LDL receptors enable the uptake of cholesterol-rich LDL by a process called receptor-mediated endocytosis (Brown and Goldstein, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown and Goldstein, 1986

claim: Lysosomal acid lipase converts cholesteryl esters from endocytosed LDL to unesterified cholesterol
source: Cells from individuals with Wolman disease or Cholesteryl Ester Storage disease revealed how lysosomal acid lipase converts cholesteryl esters liberated from the endocytosed LDL to unesterified cholesterol, a form that can be used by cells (Brown et al., 1976; Goldstein et al., 1975; Sloan and Fredrickson, 1972; Wolman et al., 1961).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brown et al., 1976; Goldstein et al., 1975; Sloan and Fredrickson, 1972; Wolman et al., 1961

claim: Chloroquine blocks the activity of lysosomal acid lipase and other lysosomal degradative processes
source: The activity of lysosomal acid lipase, and other lysosomal degradative processes, are also blocked by chloroquine (Goldstein et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goldstein et al., 1975

claim: NPC1 and NPC2 proteins move unesterified cholesterol generated by lysosomal acid lipase out of lysosomes
source: Cells from individuals with Niemann-Pick C disease revealed how two lysosomal proteins, NPC1 and NPC2, move the unesterified cholesterol generated by lysosomal acid lipase out of lysosomes (Carstea et al., 1997; Kwon et al., 2009; Liscum and Faust, 1987; Naureckiene et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carstea et al., 1997; Kwon et al., 2009; Liscum and Faust, 1987; Naureckiene et al., 2000

claim: U18666A blocks cholesterol transport out of lysosomes by binding to NPC1
source: This last step is also blocked by U18666A, a cationic amphiphile that binds to NPC1 and inhibits cholesterol transport out of lysosomes (Cenedella, 2009; Liscum and Faust, 1989; Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cenedella, 2009; Liscum and Faust, 1989; Lu et al., 2015

claim: ALOD4 is a reversible inhibitor of cholesterol transport from PM to ER
source: Here, we establish the cholesterol-binding domain 4 of anthrolysin O (ALOD4) as a reversible inhibitor of cholesterol transport from PM to endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing ALOD4 blocks PM-to-ER transport and dissociates rapidly

claim: ALOD4 depletes ER cholesterol without altering PM or overall cellular cholesterol levels
source: Using ALOD4, we: (1) deplete ER cholesterol without altering PM or overall cellular cholesterol levels
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: LDL-derived cholesterol travels from lysosomes first to PM to meet cholesterol needs, and subsequently from PM to regulatory domains of ER to suppress activation of SREBPs
source: (2) demonstrate that LDL-derived cholesterol travels from lysosomes first to PM to meet cholesterol needs, and subsequently from PM to regulatory domains of ER to suppress activation of SREBPs, halting cholesterol uptake and synthesis
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7

claim: Continuous PM-to-ER cholesterol transport allows ER to constantly monitor PM cholesterol levels and respond rapidly to small declines in cellular cholesterol by activating SREBPs
source: (3) determine that continuous PM-to-ER cholesterol transport allows ER to constantly monitor PM cholesterol levels, and respond rapidly to small declines in cellular cholesterol by activating SREBPs, increasing cholesterol uptake and synthesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript, particularly Figures 4 and 5

claim: After being synthesized in the ER, both SREBPs bind to Scap, a cholesterol-sensing membrane protein
source: After being synthesized in the ER, both SREBPs bind to Scap, a cholesterol-sensing membrane protein that escorts SREBPs from ER to Golgi when ER cholesterol levels are below a threshold level of ~5 mole% of total ER lipids (Brown and Goldstein, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown and Goldstein, 2009 and established knowledge

claim: Site-1 protease and Site-2 protease sequentially cleave SREBPs in the Golgi, generating an active transcription factor fragment
source: In the Golgi, Site-1 protease and Site-2 protease sequentially cleave SREBPs, generating an active transcription factor fragment that travels to the nucleus to upregulate lipogenic genes, eventually raising cholesterol levels in cells and in ER.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of SREBP processing pathway

claim: When ER cholesterol rises above ~5 mole% of total ER lipids, cholesterol binds to Scap and promotes Scap's binding to Insigs
source: When ER cholesterol rises above the threshold concentration of ~5 mole% of total ER lipids, cholesterol binds to Scap and promotes Scap's binding to Insigs, ER retention proteins.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of SREBP regulation pathway

claim: Equilibration of cholesterol between the bilayer leaflets of red cell membranes is rapid (t1/2 of ~1 s)
source: This step is likely not rate-limiting, since previous studies have suggested that equilibration of cholesterol between the bilayer leaflets of red cell membranes is rapid (t1/2 of ~1 s) (Steck et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Steck et al., 2002

claim: PM proteins such as ABCA1, and vesicular and non-vesicular trafficking pathways have been implicated in cholesterol movement from PM to ER
source: How cholesterol moves from PM to ER is currently not understood, although PM proteins such as ABCA1, and vesicular and non-vesicular trafficking pathways have been implicated (Holthuis and Menon, 2014; Lahiri et al., 2015; Mesmin and Maxfield, 2009; Yamauchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Holthuis and Menon, 2014; Lahiri et al., 2015; Mesmin and Maxfield, 2009; Yamauchi et al., 2015
